Zhitong Finance APP learned that Microsoft (MSFT.US) reported its fiscal first-quarter results for 2027 on Wednesday. The data showed that the company's revenue for the quarter reached $92.279 billion, up 19% year over year; GAAP net profit was $36.629 billion, a 32% increase from $27.747 billion in the same period last year; and GAAP diluted earnings per share were $4.92, compared with $3.72 in the prior-year period, up 32% year over year. Non-GAAP adjusted net profit reached $36.422 billion, up 18% year over year; adjusted earnings per share were $4.89, compared with $4.13 in the same period last year, also up 18%. Microsoft stated that its non-GAAP results exclude the impact of its investment in OpenAI. In terms of profitability, Microsoft's first-quarter operating profit reached $45.915 billion, up 21% year over year and 22% on a constant-currency basis; the operating margin was approximately 49.8%, higher than 48.9% in the same period last year. Gross profit for the quarter totaled $62.559 billion, up about 17% year over year, with a gross margin of roughly 67.8%. Microsoft Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood stated that the company posted a strong start to the new fiscal year, with Microsoft Cloud revenue reaching $63.9 billion, up 30% year over year and 31% on a constant-currency basis, marking an accelerated growth rate. The company's quarterly revenue, operating profit, and earnings per share all exceeded its internal expectations. Azure revenue grew 48%, with the cloud business continuing to benefit from AI demand. The cloud computing business continues to be a key driver of Microsoft's revenue growth. In the first fiscal quarter, Microsoft Azure revenue reached $33.165 billion, up 48% from $22.384 billion in the same period last year, reflecting the ongoing expansion of enterprise demand for cloud computing and AI infrastructure. Microsoft's cloud business generated total revenue of $63.9 billion, up 30% year over year and 31% on a constant-currency basis. Meanwhile, Microsoft's commercial backlog reached $677 billion, an increase of 73% year over year, reflecting the continued expansion of the company's pipeline of signed but not yet recognized revenue-generating commercial contracts. Microsoft 365 commercial cloud revenue grew 17% year over year, or 18% on a constant-currency basis. Adjusting for the one-percentage-point impact of revenue recognition in the prior-year period, commercial cloud revenue increased 18% year over year, or 19% on a constant-currency basis. Microsoft 365 consumer cloud revenue rose 17% year over year, while industry solutions cloud revenue grew 10% year over year. Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella stated that the company is providing customers with more powerful capabilities, greater choices, enhanced control, and more cost-effective solutions through a comprehensive technology ecosystem. Nadella pointed out that by helping enterprises build and master their own intelligent capabilities while enhancing the security and reliability of AI agents, Microsoft is driving the broader adoption of innovative technologies across industries and turning them into tangible business outcomes. Under the new business architecture, Agents and Infra revenue grew by 25%. Notably, starting from fiscal year 2027, Microsoft has adjusted its business segment structure, reclassifying its operations into two major divisions: Agents and Infra (Intelligent Agents and Infrastructure) and Devices and Consumer (Devices and Consumer Business). Among them, the Agents and Infra segment posted first-quarter revenue of $76.795 billion, up 25% year over year; operating profit reached $40.558 billion, an increase of approximately 24% from $32.718 billion in the same period last year. This segment encompasses Azure, Microsoft 365 cloud services, as well as productivity and server licensing businesses, and currently represents Microsoft's primary source of both revenue and profit. By contrast, the Devices and Consumer segment reported first-quarter revenue of $15.484 billion, down 3% year over year, with operating profit of $5.357 billion, up roughly 2% year over year. Specifically, search and advertising revenue grew 12% year over year on a constant-currency basis, excluding traffic acquisition costs; Xbox content and services revenue declined 2% year over year, or 1% on a constant-currency basis. Windows OEM and devices performed relatively weakly, with revenue down 22% year over year. By product and service category, Microsoft's first-quarter Azure revenue was $33.165 billion, while Microsoft 365 cloud business revenue reached $27.778 billion; productivity and server licensing revenue stood at $8.407 billion, search and advertising revenue was $6.554 billion, and Xbox revenue totaled $5.379 billion. OpenAI's investment gains impacted GAAP profit performance. Notably, Microsoft's GAAP net profit growth this quarter significantly outpaced its non-GAAP net profit growth, primarily due to the accounting impact of its investment in OpenAI. Microsoft disclosed that, in the first quarter of fiscal year 2027, the net gain from its investment in OpenAI boosted the company's GAAP net profit by $207 million, equivalent to a $0.03 increase in diluted earnings per share. By contrast, the net loss from the prior-year investment in OpenAI reduced the company's net profit by approximately $3.1 billion and earnings per share by $0.41. Consequently, after excluding the impact of the OpenAI investment, Microsoft's adjusted net profit for the first fiscal quarter increased 18% year over year, and adjusted earnings per share rose 18% year over year—both below the 32% growth reported under GAAP. Capital expenditures doubled year over year, and operating cash flow increased by 29%. In terms of cash flow, Microsoft's operating cash flow for the first fiscal quarter reached $58.0 billion, up approximately 29% from $45.057 billion in the same period last year. Meanwhile, the company continued to ramp up its infrastructure investments. Capital expenditures on property and equipment for the quarter totaled $39.367 billion, an increase of about 103% compared with $19.394 billion in the same period last year. On a basis that subtracts capital expenditures for property and equipment from operating cash flow, Microsoft's free cash flow for the first fiscal quarter was approximately $18.633 billion, down from $25.663 billion in the same period last year. On the balance sheet, as of September 30, 2026, Microsoft held a total of $64.509 billion in cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments, down from $76.843 billion as of June 30, 2026. In its first fiscal quarter, Microsoft returned $10.2 billion to shareholders through share repurchases and dividends, with approximately $4.379 billion spent on share repurchases and about $6.757 billion paid out in cash dividends. title: MSFT Stock Jumps Above $550 After Fiscal First-Quarter Earnings and Cloud Beat - FXLeaders
content: Microsoft stock jumped above $550 after the fiscal Q1 earnings report, as cloud growth drives earnings and revenue beat. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) shares have pulled back toward $525 after failing to establish a new record above $550. The reversal follows a rally supported by news of the company’s custom-chip development, but investors are now weighing the potential returns from Microsoft’s expanding infrastructure commitments against rising competitive and regulatory risks. The company reports fiscal first-quarter earnings today, October 28, putting its cloud business, profitability and capital expenditure plans under close scrutiny. Despite strong historical earnings growth, buyers need evidence that Microsoft’s investment strategy can deliver sustainable returns without placing excessive pressure on cash generation. Microsoft reported net income of $36.6 billion, or $4.92 per diluted share, for the quarter, representing a 32% increase on a GAAP basis. Non-GAAP earnings reached $4.89 per share, excluding the impact of investments in OpenAI. Revenue climbed to $90.6 billion from $77.6 billion a year earlier, while Wall Street had expected earnings of $4.27 per share and revenue of $90.6 billion, according to Bloomberg consensus estimates. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9 billion, increasing 30% year over year, or 31% in constant currency. Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood said results exceeded expectations across revenue, operating income and earnings per share, highlighting a strong start to the fiscal year. Chief Executive Officer Satya Nadella said Microsoft was delivering greater computing capability, customer choice and cost efficiency, while focusing on security and helping organisations develop their own AI capabilities. Revenue from Microsoft’s Devices and Consumer segment fell 3% to $15.5 billion, reflecting weakness across several businesses. Search and advertising revenue, excluding traffic acquisition costs, increased 12%. However, Xbox content and services revenue declined 2%, or 1% in constant currency, while Windows OEM and Devices revenue dropped 22%. The contrasting results highlight continued cloud strength alongside weaker demand in parts of Microsoft’s consumer and hardware businesses. Microsoft’s financial performance remains robust. Fiscal 2026 revenue increased 18% to $331.8 billion, while net income climbed 31% to $133.7 billion. However, the cost of supporting its cloud and computing expansion is becoming increasingly important to investors. Capital expenditure reached $41 billion in the fiscal fourth quarter, with approximately two-thirds directed toward shorter-lived CPUs and GPUs. Operating cash flow totalled $55.4 billion, while free cash flow stood at $19.6 billion. Capital expenditure is expected to remain above $50 billion per quarter during fiscal 2027. These commitments raise questions about how quickly Microsoft’s revenue can expand to justify the spending. Even with strong demand, the company must demonstrate that its infrastructure investments can generate attractive returns rather than simply increasing operating capacity at considerable cost. Microsoft is developing its Maia 300 processor to improve computing efficiency and reduce reliance on external chip suppliers. The processor reportedly targets 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU systems, while its 96-accelerator configuration is designed to deliver up to seven times the rack-scale throughput of Maia 200. Custom silicon could eventually help Microsoft control computing costs, although development, deployment and infrastructure expansion require substantial upfront investment. The company has also reportedly discussed leasing computing capacity from SpaceX, according to The Information, although the current status of those talks remains unclear. SpaceX expects to finish 2026 with slightly more than 2 gigawatts of computing capacity and aims to expand to between 5 GW and 10 GW next year. Microsoft’s continued capacity constraints highlight the scale of the challenge, even as spending accelerates. Microsoft shares jumped above the critical $500 level as they rebounded strongly in the last 2 months, climb above $550 earlier this week but slipped below $530 again. The price slip tested the 20 daily SMA in gray in September which has been acting as support. The $550 area represents both psychological and technical resistance so for now MAFT buyers gave up at this zone. Microsoft’s stock has undergone a notable repricing in recent months, signaling a broader reset in how investors are assessing mega-cap technology leaders. After peaking above $555 in October 2025, shares retreated sharply, and despite the revival in 2026, buyers haven’t been able to break above that level. The UK’s Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has concluded an investigation launched in May 2026 into Microsoft’s software business, including Word, Excel and Teams. The watchdog believes Microsoft should receive a strategic market status designation, potentially allowing greater regulatory scrutiny and targeted interventions. The CMA has raised concerns about the difficulty customers may face when switching providers, Microsoft’s position among approximately 20 million UK users and the competitive implications of its Copilot offering. The proposed designation does not establish wrongdoing. However, additional oversight could increase compliance costs and place restrictions on pricing, licensing or product-bundling strategies. Microsoft also faces intensifying competition from Google Workspace as businesses reassess Microsoft 365 pricing and bundled features. Maintaining its position in productivity software will require continued innovation while protecting margins. Meanwhile, the company is restructuring its gaming division, with approximately 3,200 job reductions planned during fiscal 2027, including 1,600 immediate cuts. The reductions reflect efforts to improve efficiency as Microsoft manages costs across its broader operations.

title: MSFT Stock Jumps Above $550 Ahead of Fiscal First-Quarter Earnings as Microsoft Spending Concerns Mount - FXLeaders
content: Microsoft shares jumped above $550 after the fiscal Q1 earnings report, as cloud growth drives earnings and revenue beat. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) shares have pulled back toward $525 after failing to establish a new record above $550. The reversal follows a rally supported by news of the company’s custom-chip development, but investors are now weighing the potential returns from Microsoft’s expanding infrastructure commitments against rising competitive and regulatory risks. The company reports fiscal first-quarter earnings today, October 28, putting its cloud business, profitability and capital expenditure plans under close scrutiny. Despite strong historical earnings growth, buyers need evidence that Microsoft’s investment strategy can deliver sustainable returns without placing excessive pressure on cash generation. Microsoft reported net income of $36.6 billion, or $4.92 per diluted share, for the quarter, representing a 32% increase on a GAAP basis. Non-GAAP earnings reached $4.89 per share, excluding the impact of investments in OpenAI. Revenue climbed to $90.6 billion from $77.6 billion a year earlier, while Wall Street had expected earnings of $4.27 per share and revenue of $90.6 billion, according to Bloomberg consensus estimates. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9 billion, increasing 30% year over year, or 31% in constant currency. Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood said results exceeded expectations across revenue, operating income and earnings per share, highlighting a strong start to the fiscal year. Chief Executive Officer Satya Nadella said Microsoft was delivering greater computing capability, customer choice and cost efficiency, while focusing on security and helping organisations develop their own AI capabilities. Revenue from Microsoft’s Devices and Consumer segment fell 3% to $15.5 billion, reflecting weakness across several businesses. Search and advertising revenue, excluding traffic acquisition costs, increased 12%. However, Xbox content and services revenue declined 2%, or 1% in constant currency, while Windows OEM and Devices revenue dropped 22%. The contrasting results highlight continued cloud strength alongside weaker demand in parts of Microsoft’s consumer and hardware businesses. Microsoft’s financial performance remains robust. Fiscal 2026 revenue increased 18% to $331.8 billion, while net income climbed 31% to $133.7 billion. However, the cost of supporting its cloud and computing expansion is becoming increasingly important to investors. Capital expenditure reached $41 billion in the fiscal fourth quarter, with approximately two-thirds directed toward shorter-lived CPUs and GPUs. Operating cash flow totalled $55.4 billion, while free cash flow stood at $19.6 billion. Capital expenditure is expected to remain above $50 billion per quarter during fiscal 2027. These commitments raise questions about how quickly Microsoft’s revenue can expand to justify the spending. Even with strong demand, the company must demonstrate that its infrastructure investments can generate attractive returns rather than simply increasing operating capacity at considerable cost. Microsoft is developing its Maia 300 processor to improve computing efficiency and reduce reliance on external chip suppliers. The processor reportedly targets 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU systems, while its 96-accelerator configuration is designed to deliver up to seven times the rack-scale throughput of Maia 200. Custom silicon could eventually help Microsoft control computing costs, although development, deployment and infrastructure expansion require substantial upfront investment. The company has also reportedly discussed leasing computing capacity from SpaceX, according to The Information, although the current status of those talks remains unclear. SpaceX expects to finish 2026 with slightly more than 2 gigawatts of computing capacity and aims to expand to between 5 GW and 10 GW next year. Microsoft’s continued capacity constraints highlight the scale of the challenge, even as spending accelerates. Microsoft shares jumped above the critical $500 level as they rebounded strongly in the last 2 months, climb above $550 earlier this week but slipped below $530 again. The price slip tested the 20 daily SMA in gray in September which has been acting as support. The $550 area represents both psychological and technical resistance so for now MAFT buyers gave up at this zone. Microsoft’s stock has undergone a notable repricing in recent months, signaling a broader reset in how investors are assessing mega-cap technology leaders. After peaking above $555 in October 2025, shares retreated sharply, and despite the revival in 2026, buyers haven’t been able to break above that level. The UK’s Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has concluded an investigation launched in May 2026 into Microsoft’s software business, including Word, Excel and Teams. The watchdog believes Microsoft should receive a strategic market status designation, potentially allowing greater regulatory scrutiny and targeted interventions. The CMA has raised concerns about the difficulty customers may face when switching providers, Microsoft’s position among approximately 20 million UK users and the competitive implications of its Copilot offering. The proposed designation does not establish wrongdoing. However, additional oversight could increase compliance costs and place restrictions on pricing, licensing or product-bundling strategies. Microsoft also faces intensifying competition from Google Workspace as businesses reassess Microsoft 365 pricing and bundled features. Maintaining its position in productivity software will require continued innovation while protecting margins. Meanwhile, the company is restructuring its gaming division, with approximately 3,200 job reductions planned during fiscal 2027, including 1,600 immediate cuts. The reductions reflect efforts to improve efficiency as Microsoft manages costs across its broader operations.

title: Microsoft Reports With Zero Sell Ratings and a Year of Flat Returns, We See 22% Upside - 24/7 Wall St.
content: Microsoft's revenue surged nearly 18% last year while its stock sat almost perfectly flat, and that disconnect between earnings momentum and share price tells a story most investors are missing ahead of this quarter's report. Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT | MSFT Price Prediction) goes into its fiscal first-quarter 2027 report with a ratings split that almost no mega-cap can match: 14 Strong Buy, 39 Buy, 2 Hold and zero Sell ratings. Our 24/7 Wall St. price target for Microsoft is $643.14 over the next 12 months. That means 22.62% upside, and our model rates the stock a buy with high confidence. Over the past year the stock returned only 2.66%, while fiscal 2026 revenue grew 17.79% to $331.84 billion. Results kept climbing and the share price did not follow. That gap is where I see the opportunity. Shares traded at $530.02 Monday morning. They are up 0.18% for the week, 5.88% for the month and 10.29% year to date. That leaves Microsoft 3.8% below its $551.15 52-week high and 52% above its $348.54 low. The fiscal fourth quarter drove the recovery. Revenue of $90.01 billion beat the $87.63 billion consensus, and EPS of $4.74 exceeded the $4.24 estimate. That made six straight double beats. Azure grew 43%, and commercial RPO reached $678 billion. For the current quarter, management guided to revenue of $89.85 billion to $90.95 billion and Azure growth of about 45% in constant currency. Preview coverage this week centers on whether that valuation still holds up ahead of earnings. In our bull case, the stock reaches $746.13. Demand still exceeds supply. As the CFO put it, “Customer demand continues to exceed available capacity.” Microsoft 365 Copilot passed 30 million paid seats, and net seat adds more than doubled sequentially. Microsoft is also adding usage-based billing on top of per-seat pricing. The consensus target of $601.73 stands well above today’s price. Our bear case is $544.30. Fiscal 2026 CapEx reached $115.95 billion, and free cash flow fell 6.46%. Management expects fiscal 2027 CapEx of about $175 billion (that spending has to be powered, cooled, and networked by somebody, and we covered seven of those suppliers in a free AI infrastructure report). Windows OEM and Devices revenue is expected to decline in the low 20s this quarter. Bulls would counter that operating cash flow rose 34.35%, about two-thirds of CapEx goes to short-lived chips that can be scaled back, and management expects free cash flow to stay positive in fiscal 2027. Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) is the closest AI hyperscaler comparison. The cloud business posted 82% growth, though its P/E of 14 is flattered by a $99.03 billion equity gain. Its quarterly free cash flow came in at -$5.855 billion, and buybacks are suspended. Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) runs AWS, which grew 37%. Amazon trades at a P/E of 34 with trailing free cash flow of -$7.6 billion. MSFT generates positive free cash flow and posts far higher margins, so a 24/7 Wall St. price target of about 33x trailing earnings looks reasonable to me. Microsoft earns a buy rating from our model, with a 24/7 Wall St. price target of $643.14 and 90% confidence. The deciding factor is the RPO backlog. title: Microsoft stock jumps 4% as cloud growth drives earnings and revenue beat - CNBC
content:
Microsoft shares rose 4% in extended trading on Wednesday after the company reported better-than-expected quarterly results, driven by 48% growth in its Azure cloud infrastructure business. Here’s how the company fared relative to LSEG consensus: Microsoft’s revenue grew 19% year over year in the quarter, which ended on Sept. 30, according to a statement, with Azure now its biggest single business. The software giant has been rapidly building out data center infrastructure to meet artificial intelligence demand, while also maintaining positive free cash flow unlike its fellow hyperscalers. Microsoft reported  $45.2 billion worth of capital expenditures and finance leases during the quarter, up about 30% from a year earlier. Analysts surveyed by StreetAccount had projected $50.67 billion. With respect to guidance, Microsoft called for $96 billion to $97.1 billion in fiscal second-quarter revenue, which works out to 18.8% growth at the middle of the range. Analysts polled by LSEG had predicted $95.60 billion in revenue. For Azure, Hood said she anticipates 49% to 50% growth at constant currency for the fiscal second quarter, compared with the 45.1% StreetAccount consensus. “We still have demand that exceeds supply,” she said. During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft flagged a higher growth rate for cash paid for property and equipment than overall capital expenditures, which include finance leases. “Some third-party capacity deliveries we expected in Q1 were delayed,” the company’s finance chief, Amy Hood, said on a conference call with analysts. Around 75% of capital expenditures are now tied to short-lived assets such as Intel chips and Nvidia graphics processing units, up from about 66% in the past three quarters and half in the year-ago quarter. The shift indicates Microsoft’s prioritization of infrastructure it can can quickly turn into revenue. Hood said the company is aiming at over $50 billion in fiscal second-quarter capital expenditures and finance leases, above the StreetAccount consensus of $53.10 billion, with $170 billion for all of calendar 2027 because of the capacity issues. “In the second half of the fiscal year, we currently expect capex spend to accelerate primarily from CPUs, inclusive of higher memory and storage costs, and GPUs, as well as the 3P capacity deliveries that shifted to H2,” she said. The delays have to do with GPU-as-a-service providers, she said. Free cash flow for the fiscal first quarter declined 27% to $18.63 billion. Cloud rival Alphabet reported more than $9 billion in negative free cash flow in the quarter after Meta said last week its cash flow turned negative for the first time. Microsoft will continue to generate free cash flow through the 2027 fiscal year, but the company will access additional sources of funding when it’s attractive to do so, Hood said. “We’re fortunate to have access in the debt markets, given where our rates ratings are, and sort of we haven’t been able to — we haven’t yet, I would say, tapped that,” she said. “And then, of course, there’s other options.” Microsoft’s net income increased to $36.63 billion, or $4.92 per share, from $27.75 billion, or $3.72 per share, a year ago. Adjusted earnings exclude a roughly $200 million loss on its investment in OpenAI. For the first time, Microsoft disclosed revenue from its Azure cloud in dollars, at $33.17 billion in the quarter, despite the delays from third-party providers. Analysts polled by StreetAccount expected $32.32 billion. The growth rate in the June quarter was 42%. Microsoft reported results under two operating segments — Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer.  For the past 11 years, the company had three segments that divided up its Azure, Office and Windows businesses. In Agents and Infra, revenue rose almost 25% to $76.8 billion, more than the $75.63 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount. The segment contains Azure, along with Microsoft 365 cloud products, productivity and server licensing, industry solutions and frontier and support services. The number of people using the Microsoft 365 Copilot AI assistant is up 50% from last quarter, CEO Satya Nadella said on the call. The company did not disclose the number of paid seats. The recently announced high-end Microsoft 365 E7 productivity bundle now has millions of seats, Hood said. Revenue in the Devices and Consumer business slipped 3% to $15.48 billion, beating the StreetAccount consensus of $15.05 billion. The unit includes search and advertising, Xbox, devices and Windows operating system licenses sold to device makers. Sales of devices and Windows licenses declined 22%, as higher memory and storage costs elevated prices. The company pointed to the end of support for Windows 10 last year and weak PC demand. As of Wednesday’s close, Microsoft shares were up about 10% year to date, trailing the S&P 500 index, which has gained 13% over the same period. During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft said it would cut 4,800 jobs, and followed up by announcing on Monday that it’s offering buyouts to up to 60,000 employees, as it strives to balance a costly AI build-out with capital efficiency. The AI ambitions of Amazon.com, Inc. go beyond AWS. The company is also applying artificial intelligence to warehouse automation, logistics, advertising targeting, product recommendations, and tools that help third-party sellers run their businesses more efficiently. AWS's growth rate has accelerated sharply, from 18% to 35%, a sign that Amazon.com, Inc. remains competitive even as Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud post faster growth of their own. Even so, the company still has to prove that its heavy AI investments will generate strong returns and turn into durable earnings growth (see whether Amazon's custom AI chips can outpace its capital spending). Operating leverage is a key part of the investment case, as Amazon.com, Inc. shifts toward more profitable businesses and becomes more efficient across its operations. Management expects capital spending of around $200 billion in 2026, mostly for AI infrastructure, data centers, and chips — spending large enough to push free cash flow into negative territory. Bulls see this as growth investment rather than routine maintenance spending, but it also means Amazon.com, Inc. needs strong AWS growth and sustained AI demand to justify spending at this scale over the coming years. The revenue mix of Amazon.com, Inc. is steadily shifting toward higher-value services. Advertising, third-party seller services, subscriptions, and AWS are becoming a larger part of the business relative to lower-margin first-party retail. This shift matters because it lets profits grow faster than revenue as these segments gain a bigger share of the overall mix. Based on this trajectory, expected returns work out to roughly 12.1% annualized, driven by organic growth, expanding margins, and an overall improvement in business quality. On valuation, the stock already reflects a good deal of optimism. A base-case fair value estimate puts shares of Amazon.com, Inc. around $251, with a bull-case scenario reaching $305 if revenue growth and operating margins come in stronger than expected. At current levels, the stock doesn't look dramatically overvalued, but it also doesn't offer much of a safety cushion, since investors are already paying up for faster AWS growth, AI-driven gains, and improving profitability. If AI spending falls short of expectations, AWS growth slows, or operating leverage disappoints, the premium built into the stock could come under pressure. The biggest risk to this thesis is that AI demand may stay concentrated among a small number of large customers, even as it requires enormous upfront investment. The $200 billion capital spending plan of Amazon.com, Inc. could pay off handsomely if cloud demand keeps accelerating, but weaker AI adoption, pricing pressure, or slower monetization could leave the company with high infrastructure costs and limited profit growth. Competition across cloud computing, advertising, retail, logistics, and AI — along with regulatory scrutiny — adds further uncertainty to the long-term picture. Another risk for the stock is disruption to the systems that support AWS and Amazon's wider operations. Customers rely on these services to keep applications, payments, and business processes running, making reliability central to the cloud franchise. Amazon warns that system failures or security incidents can interrupt services, cause data loss, and expose it to liability. A prolonged outage could disrupt customers and require costly remediation. Repeated incidents could also weaken confidence and make businesses more cautious about placing additional workloads on AWS. These pressures could hurt growth and profitability even if demand for AI computing remains strong. This steady rise in institutional ownership suggests hedge funds remained constructive on Amazon.com, Inc.'s AWS growth, AI opportunity, advertising business, and long-term margin expansion potential. By comparison, Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) was held by 273 hedge fund portfolios, down from 282, Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) was held by 195 hedge funds, down from 201, and Oracle Corporation (NYSE:ORCL) was held by 119 hedge funds, up from 115. The rise in ownership of Amazon.com, Inc. and Oracle Corporation, against declines for Microsoft Corporation and Alphabet Inc., points to relatively stronger institutional conviction toward Amazon.com, Inc. during the period, even as funds continue weighing its premium valuation and heavy AI spending against its long-term growth potential. Short interest data also paints a fairly calm picture for Amazon.com, Inc. relative to its peers. About 0.88% of Amazon.com, Inc.'s float is sold short, slightly higher than Microsoft Corporation at 0.82%, but below Alphabet Inc. at 1.37% and well below Oracle Corporation at 2.60%. This suggests Amazon.com, Inc. is drawing similarly limited skepticism to Microsoft Corporation, while bearish bets remain less aggressive than those against Alphabet Inc. and Oracle Corporation, even as investors weigh its valuation and capital spending. We believe the current valuation reflects expectations for AWS growth, advertising expansion, and improving margins, balanced against concerns about heavy AI spending and uncertain investment returns. However, the valuation appears reasonable rather than deeply discounted, as Amazon trades below Microsoft but above Oracle and Alphabet. AWS generated $45.6 billion in operating income in 2025, while Amazon's approximately $200 billion capital spending plan for 2026 underscores how much future growth depends on earning adequate returns from new infrastructure. We believe AMZN can justify its current valuation if higher-margin businesses sustain earnings growth while absorbing rising depreciation and financing costs. If Amazon maintains its cloud momentum and successfully turns AI investment into lasting profits and cash flow, the current valuation could offer a reasonable entry point despite the risks surrounding its infrastructure expansion. AI's high-stakes gamble faces a "cash-flow stress test" in earnings reports: Microsoft (MSFT.US) is favored, while CDS on Alphabet (GOOGL.US) have both hit record highs. Zhitong Finance APP has learned that since the last earnings report, Microsoft (MSFT.US) and Alphabet (GOOGL.US) have seen divergent stock performance, with Wall Street increasingly concerned about the drag of hefty AI spending on corporate profits. The two tech giants will release their results after the U.S. market closes on Wednesday. Recent market activity suggests investors favor Microsoft: since its July 29 earnings report revealed its cloud business posted its fastest growth in four years—sparking its best single-day performance since 2008—Microsoft's stock has surged 36%; meanwhile, Alphabet's shares have fallen 6.3% since its July 22 earnings report, which saw a sharp rise in AI-related capital expenditures leading to negative free cash flow. The market expects Google's parent company to post negative free cash flow in 2026 and 2027, while Microsoft's free cash flow is forecast to decline in its current fiscal year (ending in June) before rebounding in the foreseeable future. Luke O'Neill, portfolio manager at Catalyst Dynamic Alpha Fund, said, "Companies that can demonstrate they're generating cash for shareholders have a distinct advantage in today's market compared to those that can't," adding, "That's why Microsoft has outperformed other hyperscale cloud players over the past few months—it has shown a greater ability to navigate this environment of spending versus returns." Traders are seeking hedging protection in case hefty AI spending fails to deliver returns. Alphabet's five-year credit default swap (CDS) price hit a record high, rising 16% this month. Microsoft's five-year CDS also reached a record, climbing nearly 9% in October and on track for a fifth consecutive monthly gain—the longest winning streak on record. Both stocks underperformed the broader market this year: Microsoft rose 9.9%, and Alphabet gained 2.4%, while the S&P 500 climbed 13% and the Nasdaq 100, which is heavily weighted toward technology stocks, advanced 17%. When evaluating the spending of two companies, investors will focus on the growth of their cloud computing businesses, which is often regarded as a proxy for AI‑related demand. "It will be very reassuring to see cloud growth accelerate further, as this will bolster investors' confidence in its AI investments," said Ted Parrish, Chief Investment Officer at Parrish Capital. He holds Microsoft stock and is considering adding to his position. Earlier this week, Anthropic PBC's IPO filing highlighted the AI giant's growing reliance on cloud giants. It has also committed to spending $110 billion with Amazon by 2036, as Amazon is set to release its earnings report on Thursday. Market consensus forecasts indicate that Microsoft's Azure cloud business is expected to grow 45% at constant currency. In a report on October 14, TD Cowen analyst Derrick Wood wrote that Azure has the potential to "beat expectations by a margin above the norm" this quarter, as third-party data shows its "screening results are the strongest on record." On the Alphabet side, Google Cloud's third-quarter revenue is expected to be approximately $29 billion, up 91% from about $15 billion in the same period last year and marking a further acceleration from the 81% growth rate in the second quarter. "We're starting to see incremental returns, though this hasn't eased the pressure on its balance sheet." "Currently, the fear index is clearly highly vigilant about all these spending and ROI issues," said O'Neill of Catalyst. Microsoft "has benefited from its focus on this discipline." Its free cash flow for fiscal year 2027 is projected to be less than $32 billion, down from last year's $67 billion, before rising to $47 billion in fiscal year 2028 and $87 billion in fiscal year 2029. Given these mega‑tech companies' sustained growth, he views them as safe havens in the market. U.S.-listed shares of SK Hynix (SKHY) jumped 8% in premarket trading on Wednesday as Stephen Innes, managing partner at SPI Asset Management, highlighted how AI memory shortages are turning the company into a cash machine while technology giants face scrutiny over their spending. SKHY shares rose 2% to $145.36 but are still down 21% for October. “Right now, SK Hynix is still sitting at the toll booth, and the cash machine is humming,” Innes said on his Substack. He added that high-bandwidth memory (HBM) has become key to AI performance, boosting the Nvidia supplier’s pricing power as customers compete for limited supply. “Memory used to sit at the back of the technology factory. AI has dragged it to the front gate and handed it the keys,” he said. This puts SK Hynix in a different position from companies pouring money into AI models and data centers, Innes said. Model developers must find ways to monetize their services, while infrastructure operators face hefty power, financing and depreciation costs. The memory maker is already collecting revenue from a component they need. “SK Hynix sits on the other side of that cheque. It is already getting paid,” he said, adding: “Scarcity has a wonderful way of simplifying the income statement.” For Innes, the bigger story is in the years of production SK Hynix is securing under contract, potentially softening the pricing downturns that have historically followed memory-industry expansions. The company has signed long-term agreements with 14 major customers that cover more than half of its production capacity for 2027 and 2028. The contracts typically run five years, with extensions under discussion and prices allowed to move within agreed ranges. SK Hynix said its DRAM and HBM supply is sold out until 2029, with HBM demand double what it can supply. It expects shortages to persist through 2030. “Those contracts will not kill the cycle. Nothing kills the memory cycle. But they may blunt its teeth,” Innes said. The visibility reinforces his bigger argument that investors should distinguish between companies financing the AI buildout and those already profiting from it. “The AI trade is increasingly separating into winners who consume capital and winners who harvest it,” he said. However, Innes warned that exceptional profits will draw more competition, with Samsung and Micron expanding their HBM businesses and SK Hynix adding capacity at Yongin. “The semiconductor industry has never met a fat margin it did not eventually try to murder with new capacity,” he wrote. For Innes, the question is how long AI demand, manufacturing complexity and multiyear contracts can protect pricing power as supply grows. He argued that delivering on HBM4, securing Nvidia qualification, and maintaining spending discipline will become increasingly important. “Eventually, enough new roads will be built around the bottleneck,” he added. U.S.-listed shares of SK Hynix (SKHY) jumped 8% in premarket trading on Wednesday as Stephen Innes, managing partner at SPI Asset Management, highlighted how AI memory shortages are turning the company into a cash machine while technology giants face scrutiny over their spending. SKHY shares rose 2% to $145.36 but are still down 21% for October. “Right now, SK Hynix is still sitting at the toll booth, and the cash machine is humming,” Innes said on his Substack. He added that high-bandwidth memory (HBM) has become key to AI performance, boosting the Nvidia supplier’s pricing power as customers compete for limited supply. “Memory used to sit at the back of the technology factory. AI has dragged it to the front gate and handed it the keys,” he said. This puts SK Hynix in a different position from companies pouring money into AI models and data centers, Innes said. Model developers must find ways to monetize their services, while infrastructure operators face hefty power, financing and depreciation costs. The memory maker is already collecting revenue from a component they need. “SK Hynix sits on the other side of that cheque. It is already getting paid,” he said, adding: “Scarcity has a wonderful way of simplifying the income statement.” For Innes, the bigger story is in the years of production SK Hynix is securing under contract, potentially softening the pricing downturns that have historically followed memory-industry expansions. The company has signed long-term agreements with 14 major customers that cover more than half of its production capacity for 2027 and 2028. The contracts typically run five years, with extensions under discussion and prices allowed to move within agreed ranges. SK Hynix said its DRAM and HBM supply is sold out until 2029, with HBM demand double what it can supply. It expects shortages to persist through 2030. “Those contracts will not kill the cycle. Nothing kills the memory cycle. But they may blunt its teeth,” Innes said. The visibility reinforces his bigger argument that investors should distinguish between companies financing the AI buildout and those already profiting from it. “The AI trade is increasingly separating into winners who consume capital and winners who harvest it,” he said. However, Innes warned that exceptional profits will draw more competition, with Samsung and Micron expanding their HBM businesses and SK Hynix adding capacity at Yongin. “The semiconductor industry has never met a fat margin it did not eventually try to murder with new capacity,” he wrote. For Innes, the question is how long AI demand, manufacturing complexity and multiyear contracts can protect pricing power as supply grows. He argued that delivering on HBM4, securing Nvidia qualification, and maintaining spending discipline will become increasingly important. “Eventually, enough new roads will be built around the bottleneck,” he added. History says to respect the tails. MSFT’s actual move exceeded the implied move in four of the last eight reports, including a 16% surge in April 2025 and a 13.4% jump last July. Azure remains the engine of the story. Microsoft’s cloud platform grew 43% in fiscal Q4 and crossed $100 billion in annual revenue for the first time, and management has guided to 44% to 45% growth this quarter. Intelligent Cloud revenue is guided to $40.95 billion to $41.25 billion, up 33% to 34%. Commercial RPO, the contracted revenue not yet recognized, hit $678 billion last quarter. Excluding OpenAI, it still grew 25%, which matters because concentration risk with OpenAI has been a persistent concern since early this year. Management has also said repeatedly that demand continues to exceed available capacity, so Azure growth is a function of how fast Microsoft can bring GPUs and data centers online. Capital spending is where the bull and bear debates collide. Microsoft spent $41 billion on capex in fiscal Q4, roughly two thirds on short-lived assets like GPUs and CPUs, and has guided to more than $50 billion this quarter. Calendar 2026 capex is expected to land near $175 billion. Heavy depreciation has already pressured margins: gross margin slipped to 67.6% in fiscal Q3, the lowest since 2022, and cloud gross margin was 65% last quarter. Microsoft still guided operating margin roughly flat year over year, so any slippage there will draw attention. The macro backdrop adds pressure. AI-linked stocks sold off on October 8 after a report that OpenAI’s revenue was lower than expected, and again on October 22, when MSFT fell 2.2%. Why are technology stocks rising so much and is it really a good time to buy them? Before getting into our analysis, let's take a look at the business and why some investors like the stock so much. Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) remains one of the largest technology companies in the world, and the current investment debate is shifting from whether Apple can keep growing to whether its high valuation is justified as it becomes a slower-growth but more dependable technology stock. Apple reported record revenue of $109.42 billion, 16% higher than last year, with iPhone sales up 22% and earnings per share of $2.02, beating expectations. Despite these strong results, the stock fell 7.35% after earnings and kept slipping as investors focused less on what Apple just delivered and more on what it expects next: 9%-11% growth, below the 12% analysts were hoping for. With the stock trading at around 35 times earnings, that gap between a rich valuation and a slowing growth outlook is what's rattling investors. Read More: 15 AI Stocks That Are Quietly Making Investors Rich Read More: Undervalued AI Stock Poised For Massive Gains: 10000% Upside Potential The bullish case for Apple isn't built on it becoming an AI powerhouse, but on it being a safer way to stay invested in technology. While companies like Nvidia, Amazon, and Microsoft are pouring money into AI infrastructure with all the risks that come with a spending boom, Apple offers exposure to tech without betting on that cycle. Its ecosystem of iPhones, services, and wearables gives it a steady, reliable base that can keep rewarding shareholders over time, even without chasing the AI trade. The recent slowdown looks more like a supply problem than a demand problem. Apple said that memory chips, DRAM and NAND, are increasingly being funneled toward AI data centers as that industry snaps up components, which has forced Apple to limit some higher-memory device configurations. In other words, this is about chip supply being stretched thin industry-wide, not about weaker interest in Apple's products. If investors eventually look past the AI hype and back toward companies with consistent execution, Apple's steady approach could start looking more appealing. Apple's case also depends on it continuing to execute reliably even as growth slows, (see whether Apple's 35x valuation is getting ahead of its growth) and that's the piece investors will be watching closely. The real question is whether a company growing more slowly than many of its tech peers deserves to trade at such a rich multiple. Those in favor of the premium point to Apple's strong cash generation, consistent shareholder returns, and one of the most powerful consumer ecosystems in the world. But if earnings growth doesn't keep up, the market may become less willing to pay up for that stability. That said, slower growth is the biggest risk to this story. The current 9%-11% guidance may just reflect temporary supply issues, but if growth stays stuck in the single digits for longer, investors may start to worry it's a deeper problem rather than a short-term hiccup. At the same time, Apple's valuation doesn't leave much room for missteps. Adding to the uncertainty is an upcoming CEO transition, though incoming leader John Ternus brings around 25 years at Apple and a strong hardware and product background, which could help him navigate supply chain issues and future product launches. Another risk for the stock is regulatory pressure on the App Store's business model. Apple's ecosystem supports repeat spending, but regulators and courts are challenging how it controls app distribution and collects commissions. title: Microsoft offers voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees as AI leads to efficiency push - CNBC
content:
Microsoft said Monday that it’s offering buyouts to a wide swath of employees as it strives to balance a costly artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out with capital efficiency. The software maker announced a new voluntary exit offer for certain workers in the U.S., Canada, India and the United Kingdom at its experience level of 70 or below. Around 60,000 people are eligible, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named while discussing an internal matter. The effort affects about 27% of Microsoft’s total workforce of 223,000 people. Microsoft has been ramping up spending on data centers to accommodate high AI computing demand, supplying cloud services to Anthropic, OpenAI and a slew of other companies. Capital expenditures for the September quarter should exceed $50 billion, Microsoft said in July. In the same quarter a year ago, capital spending and finance leases came to $34.9 billion. That’s put a strain on Microsoft’s finances. In April, it announced a first-ever voluntary retirement program that around 7% of U.S. employees were eligible for. Then, in July, Microsoft announced plans to lay off 4,800 employees. “The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we’re evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter,” Amy Coleman, Microsoft’s executive vice president and chief people officer, wrote in a memo to employees. “This builds on what we learned earlier this year through the Voluntary Retirement Program.” Microsoft is in the midst of a business model transformation, increasingly trying to charge clients based on how much AI they actually use. It has armed programmers, sellers and supply chain workers with AI tools and observed noticeable results. At the same time, the 51-year-old maker of Windows and Office wants to ensure that it has the right talent to go after its most compelling new growth opportunities. The idea is to make the shift without weakening Microsoft’s financial profile. In the second quarter, cloud rivals Alphabet and Amazon both reported negative free cash flow, but Microsoft showed $19.64 billion in positive free cash flow for the period, down 23% year over year. Some marketing, sales and engineering teams have decided not to participate in the new buyout, the person said. Employees must decide whether to take the offer in early December, and those participating will leave on Dec. 31, the person added. More than 30% of those who could join the voluntary retirement program went ahead with it, Microsoft said in July. But that was open to those at the senior director level of 67 and below, while the new initiative goes higher, to the vice president level, said the person briefed on the new plan. The person said Microsoft does not have a target in mind this time around. On Wednesday, Microsoft is scheduled to report third-quarter results. content: Microsoft Corp.(MSFT) is launching a workforce reduction initiative, extending voluntary buyout offers to approximately 60,000 employees, Bloomberg reported. According to the report, the move is designed to control operational expenditures and retool personnel capabilities to match the rapidly expanding artificial intelligence landscape. A company spokesperson told Bloomberg that the buyout option applies to personnel at the vice president level and below within designated teams across the United States, Canada, India, and the United Kingdom. However, specific operational units—including certain groups tied to data centers, sales, and marketing—are excluded from the current round. Chief People Officer Amy Coleman addressed staff in an internal memorandum on Monday, noting that the initiative provides a structured exit path with corporate backing for those contemplating a career shift outside the company. Participating workers will receive benefits mirroring standard severance terms. Microsoft's total headcount stood at roughly 223,000 at the close of June. Total employee figures have remained relatively flat since 2022. While Microsoft previously executed a voluntary buyout targeting retirement-age staff in July, which saw over 30% of the 8,750 eligible workers accept, company representatives expect a significantly smaller proportion of personnel to take up the new, broader proposal. Microsoft is not alone in its efforts to adjust its workforce to accommodate the AI boom. Competitors have similarly reduced headcounts to redirect capital into heavy-duty data infrastructure. Meta Platforms Inc. has trimmed its staff significantly from its late 2022 peak, while Google implemented voluntary buyout initiatives across several divisions. Tech executives increasingly emphasize a faster operational tempo and an explicit commitment to rapid technological change. Coleman emphasized in her memo that the buyout framework gives individual Microsoft divisions an alternative way to adjust their labor pools to shifting corporate demands. Macro analyst Michael Howell said on Monday that Bitcoin (BTC) holding above $70,000 could be a “game changer” for his outlook on global liquidity, while explaining that Bitcoin tends to beat gold when the U.S. Federal Reserve adds liquidity faster than China’s central bank. Speaking on the Bankless podcast, Howell, a global liquidity expert and the Managing Director at GL Indexes, said his base case was still that global liquidity will not bottom until the second half of 2027. However, he said Bitcoin’s recent stability could be an early signal of a turn. “If you get Bitcoin holding above 70,000, if you see more evidence that bank reserves are being managed and maybe being pushed up, then I would powerfully change my view and expect to see liquidity picking up,” Howell said. In that case, Bitcoin could be signaling the early stages of “another two to three year bull market,” he added. He stressed, “It’s not my base case.” Bitcoin was among the top trending crypto tickers on Stocktwits at the time of writing. Howell’s comments came as Bitcoin’s price traded around $79,600 on Monday, nearly 14% above the $70,000 level he flagged. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around BTC remained in the ‘bearish’ zone, while chatter stayed at ‘normal’ levels over the past day. Howell said in the interview that Chinese money printing has been the main driver of gold’s rise. “It’d be great to put more money into gold.” he said, adding that “Look at China’s warping great trade surface.” Citing Richard Nixon, Howell pointed out that “I mean, we talk about debasement, but broadly speaking, ever since Richard Nixon closed the gold window back in 1971, you effectively had free-floating currencies and ongoing debasement, or certainly accelerated displacement, one would say.” Adding to it he said, “Paradoxically, the U.S. is moving more towards the Chinese model than maybe many people would like, and this is big government, big state.” Writing on Substack, Howell added that “Bitcoin tends to outperform gold when Fed Liquidity grows faster than PBoC Liquidity,” referring to the People’s Bank of China. He asked whether the Bitcoin-gold ratio was becoming a “scoreboard” for America versus China. Howell warned that there may be “further weakness in coming months,” but said he would buy on dips. “I think Bitcoin is going to go up because the liquidity cycle is going to turn,” he said. He suggested holding both Bitcoin and gold. “They both work. Why don’t you just own both?” he asked. He said he would weigh the mix by volatility, holding more gold for now. As Bitcoin becomes more institutional, “its volatility will come down, and therefore you can increase your weighting over time,” Howell said. Bloomberg Intelligence senior commodity strategist Mike McGlone also focused on the Bitcoin-gold ratio. He said Bitcoin “has bounced from its earlier-in-the-year swoon to key inflection levels vs. gold, U.S. Treasury bonds and the S&P 500 (SPX).” McGlone warned of “greater downside risks” unless Bitcoin “can recover from its relative-dud performer status of almost five years.” His chart shows the ratio near 20, a level he flagged as key, adding that Bitcoin “may need higher stocks” to clear it.
